passages.t: A good name, one Maker, and training a child
passages.happening:
“A good name is more desirable than great riches; favor is better than silver and gold” (verse 1). “The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is Maker of them all” (verse 2). ‘The prudent see danger and take cover, but the simple keep going and suffer the consequences’ (verse 3). ‘The rewards of humility and the fear of the LORD are wealth and honor and life’ (verse 4).

Then one of the best-known sayings in the book: “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it” (verse 6).

‘The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender’ (verse 7). ‘He who sows injustice will reap disaster’ (verse 8). And ‘A generous man will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
These verses are near the end of the long collection of Solomon's proverbs, which closes at verse 16. Its last sayings gather around wealth and poverty.

Verse 2 puts rich and poor on the same ground. Whatever separates them, they share one Maker.

Verse 7 states a hard fact. A person who could not repay a debt could be forced into servitude, and creditors could even take children as payment. The law limited such servitude and required release in the seventh year, but the danger was real. The saying describes it. It does not approve of it.
passages.later: The Bible shows how real verse 7 was. A prophet's widow cried to Elisha that her husband's creditor ‘is coming to take my two children as his slaves’ (2 Kings 4:1). And Ezekiel insists that each generation answers for itself: ‘A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son’ (Ezekiel 18:20).
passages.hard:
Verse 6 says a well-trained child will not depart from the way. What about faithful parents whose children walk away?

This verse has brought comfort to many parents and deep pain to others, especially when it is read as a promise that good parenting guarantees a faithful child. That reading misunderstands what a proverb is. Like the rest of the collection, verse 6 describes how life usually goes: early training tends to shape a whole life. It is a true and hopeful pattern, not a contract.

Proverbs itself shows that children make their own choices. It keeps warning sons who were taught well not to leave their teaching (19:27). Scripture tells of good parents with wayward children and of troubled parents with faithful ones, and Ezekiel 18 says that each generation answers for its own choices.

Readers also differ on what ‘the way he should go’ means. Many read it as the moral and spiritual way of wisdom. Others read it as training suited to the child's own character or stage of life. A few read the verse as ironic, a warning: let a child go his own way, and he will never leave it.

On any reading, the verse urges parents to take their task seriously. It does not make them the only cause of a child's faith or unbelief, and it does not allow anyone to blame grieving parents for a grown child's choices.
passages.asks: A good name is worth more than riches. Ask what name you are building, at home and at work. And if you are a parent whose child has walked away, ask God for the patience to keep loving and praying, knowing this verse does not lay the blame on you.

passages.t: The slacker's lion, and the rod of discipline
passages.happening:
‘Drive out the mocker, and conflict will depart; even quarreling and insults will cease’ (verse 10). ‘He who loves a pure heart and gracious lips will have the king for a friend’ (verse 11). The LORD watches over knowledge and frustrates the faithless (verse 12).

The slacker makes an excuse to stay indoors: there is a lion outside, he says, and he will be killed in the street (verse 13). ‘The mouth of an adulteress is a deep pit’ (verse 14).

“Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him” (verse 15). And the collection of Solomon's proverbs ends with a warning: ‘Oppressing the poor to enrich oneself or giving gifts to the rich will surely lead to poverty’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The slacker of verse 13 is a comic figure. He invents dangers to avoid work. A lion in the street is the most dramatic excuse he can think of.

Verse 15 says that folly is tied up in a child's heart. Children are not born wise. They have to be taught, and correction is part of how they learn. The rod, shevet, also names a shepherd's staff and a ruler's scepter, and Proverbs uses it of correcting adult fools as well as sons.

With verse 16 the collection that began at 10:1 comes to an end. The scholars who count it note that it holds exactly 375 verses.
passages.later: Paul gives fathers a limit that belongs beside verse 15: “Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21).
passages.hard:
Does verse 15 tell parents to strike their children?

Faithful Christian parents read this verse, with 13:24, 23:13-14 and 29:15, in two main ways, and both deserve a fair hearing.

Many take it as instruction for parents. For them, measured physical discipline of a young child, given calmly and in love, never in anger and never to injure, is one way of driving out the folly the verse names, and it is then over. They stress that the verse's target is the folly, not the child.

Others read the rod as a picture of correction in general, since the same book uses the rod of adult fools, and they hold that Proverbs describes the methods of its own culture rather than a technique for every age. They correct through consequences, teaching and close relationship, and they point to the New Testament's word to fathers not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21).

This question divides faithful parents without dividing anyone from Christ. These notes take no side.

Both agree on the most important things. The aim is a child's good, not a parent's anger. Correction given in anger, or that injures a child, is not discipline at all. Nothing in this verse gives anyone a warrant to harm a child, and the whole Bible condemns injury and abuse.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The slacker invents a lion to stay home. Ask what excuse you have been using to avoid something you know you should do. And if you are a parent, ask whether the correction in your home is aimed at your child's good, and given with patience.

passages.t: The words of the wise: listen, and trust the LORD
passages.happening:
A new voice begins. ‘Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise’ (verse 17). Keep them within you and on your lips (verse 18). “So that your trust may be in the LORD” (verse 19), the teacher has written them. ‘Have I not written for you thirty sayings about counsel and knowledge’ (verse 20), to show what is true and reliable (verse 21).

Then come the sayings. ‘Do not rob a poor man because he is poor, and do not crush the afflicted at the gate, for the LORD will take up their case and will plunder those who rob them’ (verses 22-23). ‘Do not make friends with an angry man’ (verse 24), or you may learn his ways and be trapped (verse 25). ‘Do not be one who gives pledges, who puts up security for debts’ (verse 26).

‘Do not move an ancient boundary stone which your fathers have placed’ (verse 28). “Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will be stationed in the presence of kings” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
This is a seam in the book. A new section, the Words of the Wise, runs to 24:22. Its form is different: longer units, often a command and a reason, with the teacher speaking directly to ‘you’, like the father of chapters 1 to 9. And verse 19 states the purpose of the whole: that your trust may be in the LORD.

This section has a famous parallel. In the 1920s scholars published an Egyptian work, the Instruction of Amenemope, written by an official for his son in thirty chapters. Its sayings closely resemble parts of 22:17 to 23:11: listening carefully, not robbing the poor or crushing the afflicted, avoiding the hot-tempered man, not moving the ancient boundary stone, and the skilled scribe fit to stand before kings. Most scholars think Israel's sages knew it and adapted it. A minority think both drew on a common tradition. Either way, the Israelite version sets the advice under trust in the LORD and makes the LORD the defender of the poor.

Verse 20's ‘thirty’ is a puzzle. The Hebrew letters have been read as formerly, as excellent things, or as thirty, which most modern translations adopt partly because of Amenemope's thirty chapters.

Family land was marked by stones set up generations earlier. Moving one at night could quietly shift part of a field from a weak family to a strong one. The gate was where the town's court met, and the poor, with no one to speak for them, were easily wronged there.
passages.later: The law cursed what verse 28 forbids: ‘Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundary stone’ (Deuteronomy 27:17). And James asks, ‘Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him?’ (James 2:5).
passages.asks: The teacher wrote all this so that your trust may be in the LORD. Ask whether the advice you follow, from any source, is leading you to trust him more. And ask who near you is like the poor at the gate, with no one to take up their case.
